value: most sensitive at 3.2 kHz, with in-air thresholds of 13 and 14 dB re 20 uPa in the two sea lions
method: behavioural go/no-go audiometry, tone level lowered and raised in 6 dB steps (staircase), threshold taken as the mean of the reversal levels, in a soundproofed room with an anechoic chamber built inside it at Taronga Zoo, Sydney
conditions: two adult females, Nala (zoo-born, 17 years old) and Tarni (wild-born, 10 years old); tone frequencies 100 Hz to 20 kHz, each frequency tested in three sessions with the lowest threshold reported; the two audiograms were similar at 800 to 3200 Hz, and Tarni was less sensitive than Nala at lower and higher frequencies (Table 1: Nala 72 and Tarni 85 dB at 100 Hz, Nala 27 and Tarni 51 dB at 20 kHz); Tarni's 20 dB bandwidth of best sensitivity ran from about 600 Hz to 9 kHz and Nala's reached at least 20 kHz, the top of the tested range (tones above 20 kHz could not be projected), so her upper limit is not measured; Table 1 gives Nala 13 and Tarni 14 dB at 3.2 kHz; ambient noise in the chamber at 3.2 kHz was 11 dB re 20 uPa (1/3-octave band level), 2 to 3 dB below these thresholds, and the paper's critical-ratio argument against masking is made only at 6.4, 12.8 and 20 kHz (it says the lowest level the animals responded to was 14 dB, which disagrees with Nala's 13 dB in Table 1); 30 to 50% of trials were catch trials, and false alarm rates were about 20% for Nala and 35% for Tarni

value: cavefish (Pachon morph) have lower, i.e. better, olfactory detection thresholds than surface fish overall
eye: olfactory epithelium (waterborne amino acids and chondroitin, attraction behaviour)
method: behavioural attraction test in pools: fish counted in the odour half and the water half of the pool every 15 s and scored as a preference index from -1 to 1
conditions: lab-raised adult Pachon cavefish compared with surface fish and F1 hybrids; wild cavefish were also tested in five caves (Pachon, Sabinos, Tinaja, Chica, Subterraneo), but wild surface fish could not be tested in the field; field pools held 8 fish each (n = 24 per cave visit, 3 pools), lab tests used 8 pools of 8 fish per morph (64 fish), run in the dark (IR recording) by three experimenters, blinding not stated; adult Lab-Pachon were attracted by alanine at 1e-7 M and Lab-SF only at 1e-5 M; surface fish and hybrids were tested only in the lab; ages of the lab adults are not given; the odorants were alanine, serine and chondroitin: chondroitin attracted all lab morphs (Lab-Pachon more intensely), serine elicited very little response in surface or cave adults (no morph comparison given), and the Discussion also says 'The adult Lab-SF had a lower olfactory detection threshold than the Lab-Pachón' (Section 4.2), which the paper does not reconcile with the Section 3.2 adult alanine result favouring Lab-Pachon; wild Chica fish did not respond to the odours tested; the quote gives no concentration, and the threshold concentrations (larval alanine and serine thresholds near 1e-5 M surface and 1e-10 M Pachon; Pachon chondroitin threshold 1e-4 M) were read in a page-summary paraphrase and are not filed

value: Pekin ducks, unlike Muscovy ducks, were conditioned to discriminate inedible objects of the same size and shape but different hardness with the bill
method: operant two-bowl conditioning: worms paired with hard plastiline cylinders in the rewarded bowl and soft plastiline cylinders of the same type in the unrewarded bowl; success criterion was foraging in the correct bowl in under 20 s on three consecutive trials
conditions: domestic Pekin duck (Anas platyrhynchos domestica, hatched on site from eggs bought from a farm), tested beside Muscovy ducks (Cairina moschata domestica, shipped as day-old ducklings; Muscovy not filed here); ducks raised 4 months in one aviary and 4 months in another, tested at the onset of sexual maturity, exact ages not given; the number of ducks of each species on the hardness task is not stated (only ducks successful on the earlier task went on, and six females and one male per species learned that earlier task, more females than males, Chi2 = 16.7, p < 0.0001); in the unrewarded test Pekins spent on average 76% of the time foraging in the correct (hard-plastiline) bowl (t = 4.6, df = 8, p < 0.005) and Muscovies 27%, spending significantly more time in the soft-plastiline bowl (t = 3.3, df = 6, p < 0.05), Pekin against Muscovy t = 3.9, df = 7, p < 0.01; the species also foraged differently on this task (Pekins deep dabbling, Muscovies surface dabbling, Kruskal-Wallis p < 0.001), so the Muscovy result may reflect foraging strategy as well as tactile discrimination; hard Roma plastiline against soft Prima Plastilina, no hardness values measured; both species learned to associate hard plastiline distractors with reward, and Muscovy ducks failed only the unrewarded test; females learned the conditioning tasks faster than males across both species (not specific to the hardness task); the quote gives no hardness values
